title: Doubly Burdened, Dually Strained:  The Strategic Utilization of Chicago’s Community Health Workers in Task-Shifting Interventions
abstract: Drawing on ethnographic research approaches including semi-structured qualitative interviews and participant-observation, in this thesis I examine how Black and Latina Community Health Workers (CHWs) in Chicago navigate their mandate to influence peer health behaviors and build bridges with underserved groups. Often associated with settings of poverty and limited infrastructure in the Global South, CHW programs—a mode of “task-shifting” key health care services from specialists to less expensive labor—are increasingly implemented as a possible solution to persistent and acute health disparities in the metropolises of the Global North. Because CHWs are active members of the community in which they serve, they provide a crucial link between health providers and those communities that face barriers to clinical space. This is especially true in communities where histories of abuse and mistrust define the provider-patient relationship. This thesis demonstrates that CHWs’ identities as members of these marginalized communities play an important role in how they approach their mission and complicates reductive visions of CHWs harmoniously disseminating information, increasing healthcare use, and re-forging relations of trust between health systems and vulnerable people. The CHWs I encountered struggled with tensions between local knowledge and values and the burden of increasing the utilization of systems that they know to be flawed and unequal, underscoring that task-shifting is no magic bullet for inequalities with complex and long-standing determinants. I use these findings to call into question the potentials and limitations of CHW programs, highlighting the counter-intuitive positionalities that pull at either end of community identity and workforce expectations. This study contributes to the ongoing discussion of dissemination of health information to underserved populations and provides recommendations for more effective implementation of task-shifting approaches in the future.
